title: I Got 99 Essays, But a Throughline Ain't One
text: Nye's Digital Lab is a weekly scribble on creativity in an age of rapid change. This week I'm reading myself. I have carefully avoided doing that for three years and 129,000 words. Subscribe High level analysis of my library of essays. Source Claude Opus 5.5. Essay #100! The Robots Read Me This week is my 100th essay, so... I let the robots read me. Not one essay. All of them. About 129,000 words. I split the pile between four models, gave each one twenty-five or so essays, and asked one question: What does this guy keep saying? I wanted a pattern. Some sign of what Nye's Digital Lab is actually about. I hate rereading my essays. I write them, I publish them on Sunday, and I move on . Going back feels like hearing my voice on a voicemail. I did read some of them. But, I had the machines do most of it. And the first thing they showed me wasn't an idea. It was a calendar. The Digital Lab didn't start as a weekly practice. It started as a blog in January 2023. I wrote eight essays that year, and then went quiet for eight months. In 2024 I wrote seven, with three gaps longer than two and a half months. Those first fifteen essays took me almost two years. Then, on March 30, 2025, something changed. I published Here Comes Reinforcement Learning , and I haven't gone more than two weeks without an essay since . Every Sunday of 2026 has one. The blog years were me waiting until I had something worth saying. The weekly years are me saying something, and finding out on the page if it was worth it. I am literally just jumping ahead of myself and pushing publish. Anyway, here are the five ideas I seem to talk about the most in 99 essays of Nye's Digital Lab. The Five Ideas One. Judgment survives. When execution is free, judgment is what's left. (19 essays) It's the DJ who doesn't just drop the needle. It's " you do not create with AI, you search. " It's the hours migrating from the fingers to the ear. Last week, I said it was whoever people trust to pick the shot. I've said this in every lane I write in, in three different vocabularies. It's my most repeated idea, and maybe my most self-serving. According to AI, I almost never say taste . I say trust . Whoever people trust to pick the shot. Maybe judgment isn't the skill. Maybe it's the reputation you build by showing up. The best example: Helmets and Violins — Judgment. The frontier models are the biggest sampler ever built, and the hours migrate from the fingers to the ear. Two. You have to earn it. The friction was the education. (15 essays) Count before the calculator. Beat the boss without the automation. Sand the friction away and you get a faster tourist. I fully wrote one of these by hand, in August, in a cold sweat. I think this is the whole academic crisis in one line. We don't need more AI literacy. We need to teach people the grit to survive what's coming. The Graphics Hack — Earn it. Two doors, and I'm standing between them. Three. Open beats closed. The edge beats the cloud, and the bubble pops. (23 essays) My widest thread, and really two bets wearing one coat. The first half held. Open models sit a few months behind the frontier. A fixed unit of intelligence gets ten times cheaper every year. Six in ten tokens on the biggest marketplace now run on Chinese open weights. The second half, the collapse, I've been calling since Universal Basic Compute . The capex I called a bubble in April doubled by September. And we all seem to still run Claude Code every single day. I still think the big bubble goes boom . I just don't know when. The Big Bang — Open beats closed. The bubble I wanted to pop, and it hasn't. Four. The work moves. It doesn't disappear, and the schools that stall get merged. (18 essays) Detroit, then Hollywood. The sawed-off first rung. Merge before you're merged. The gone half of this claim is the best-evidenced thing I've written. The moved half I've asserted eighteen times and shown zero. Bangalore. Micro-studios. Utility players. Those are the places I said the work would go. The one number I actually checked cuts the other way. Twenty thousand games on Steam last year. Six hundred got a thousand reviews. My Heart Bleeds for Hollywood — The work moves. Detroit, one industry earlier. Five. The ledger pays artists. Attribution by name will pay the artists, and the ledger is how. (15 essays) This was actually the reason I started writing. I felt that artists should be compensated for their ideas. Six of my first eight essays. I've apologized for it in print at least seven times, and re-prescribed it every single time. Yes, it's true. I believe in the blockchain. Aaaaand ... I feel really bad about it. Notice this essay is cryptographically secured on Paragraph, a blockchain based platform. I am here for a reason . The Ghost of Napster — The ledger. The founding claim, with its dated predictions attached. Share And The Analysis Here's some of the data. The machines also built me a map! Every dot is an essay. Essays that use similar words sit close together. The top panel colors each essay by the folder I filed it in. The bottom colors it by what the text actually says. Where they disagree, my filing and my writing disagree. Here's the coolest stuff (I think). There are no walls. The essays don't split into clean topics. Teaching and personal are the same lane. When you read the words, my education essays and my personal essays blend together. The teaching essays are the personal essays. I didn't know that! "AI" is not a topic. My AI & Technology essays don't resemble each other any more than they resemble everything else. AI is a constant. Only robots stick together. Robotics is the one folder where the essays actually sound alike. Everything else wanders. Almost a third of the essays live in the wrong house. For 30 of 97 essays, the three closest essays by text are all filed somewhere else. Personal Reflection is the worst. I write in runs. Consecutive essays are more alike than random pairs. The Sunday essay is usually a continuation of last Sunday's. So, apparently I am literally all over the map. Just Keep Showing Up So I have 99 essays, and a throughline ain't one. I used three major AI models, a similarity map, and a pile of tables to find out what I believe. The answer was in the calendar. Nothing got clear when I had a big idea. It got clear when I started writing every week. You need to do the work. That's it. That's the throughline. Show up on Sunday. Write the thing. Do it again. I was wrong about Jay-Z. Maybe it's the other guy: Woody Allen. 80% of success is showing up. I'll settle for every week if I can keep this up. Until next time. Make it Happen. Colophon This essay was constructed from a deep dive analysis of the past 99 essays from Nye's Digital Lab using Claude Fable 5.1, Gemini 3 Pro / 3.1 Pro, and Deep Seek v4. Additional revisions were done by a human pushing buttons on a keyboard. Nye Warburton is an artist and educator from Savannah, GA. For more information: nyewarburton.com Subscribe

title: The Cost Collapse
text: Nye's Digital Lab is a weekly scribble on creativity in an age of rapid change. Share A Shot a Day Most of my career was spent making movies nobody was allowed to see. Previsualization (known as 'previs' for short) is the rough draft of a film, built in 3D before anyone builds anything real. Gray blob actors. Cameras that fly through walls. Every big movie on my resume, and there are a few big ones, went through a version of itself that looked like a video game from 1998. The measure was speed not quality. In finals, a visual effects artist might get weeks on one shot. In previs you're doing at least shot a day, often times, many more. You learn to stop being so friggin' precious. That pace did something to the economics that I don't think anyone really planned. The most expensive mistake in visual effects is finding out a shot doesn't work after you've built it. Previs let a director find that out in gray boxes, in a day, for almost nothing. So effects got cheaper per shot. A lot cheaper. But if you notice, the movies did not get cheaper. Not once. The studios pocketed the savings and bought more stuff. More shots, bigger sequences, whole third acts made of explosions of pixels. The effects budget went up while the price per shot went down. We spent the same and got absurdly more. I bring this up because the next version is aimed right at the next generation. Television Wars, Leonardo/Flow State Zenith Let's talk about televisions. In 1960 there were twenty-seven American companies making TVs. Zenith and RCA had about a fifth of the market each. By the end of 1987 there was one American TV maker left. Japan didn't win with a better picture tube. It won with the unglamorous stuff. Scale. Owning the whole supply chain. Building so many factories they had to export to keep the lines running. Sony's first pocket radio hit the States in 1957 for $39.95, and Akio Morita turned down a giant order to sell it under an American store's brand. He wanted his own name on the box. America tried to stop it. First came accusations that Japan was dumping cheap sets below cost. Then, in 1977, a deal that capped Japanese TV imports at 1.75 million a year. But, It didn't matter. Sony had been building televisions in San Diego since 1972. Matsushita bought Motorola's TV business and kept selling the same sets under the name Quasar. A set built in California isn't an import. The wall went up, and the factories just walked around it. Zenith is the one you should be looking at. Consumer Reports rated its sets among the best built all through the seventies. The quality was real. And in the middle of that, Zenith laid off half its research engineers. It kept the name on the box and fired the people who knew how to make the next box. OK, now let's do cars. Chinese Cars. BYD sells an electric car in China for under ten thousand dollars. Chinese battery packs run about a third cheaper than ours, and Chinese factories can make roughly three times the batteries the planet buys. Europe put up tariffs to stop them. The US put up a hundred percent tariff! Volkswagen's margin dropped under one percent for a quarter. And just like Quasar did in the 70's with TVs, the factories are walking around the wall again. One of them, Hyundai , is a short drive from my house. I've watched this movie. I know how this goes. Tokens How about some numbers and some predictions, Nye? Since late 2022, the price of a fixed unit of AI intelligence has been dropping about ten times a year. Not 10%, Ten TIMES! What cost twenty dollars then costs forty cents now. Batteries are supposed to be the miracle of cheap. They fell eight percent last year. And the same players are running the same play. By this spring, about six in ten of the AI words moving through the biggest independent model marketplace came from Chinese open models. Nearly as good, a tenth of the price. Every update from the frontier seems to get an open Chinese version, merely weeks after. When the first cheap Chinese model dropped, Wall Street panicked and sold Nvidia. Wrong target, folks. The chip makers are fine. The people getting squeezed are the brand names in the middle, the ones who thought the name on the box was the business. Animation is where my heart bleeds. Jeffrey Katzenberg once said it took 500 artists five years to make a world-class animated movie, and last year he said that he expected that to shrink by ninety percent. OpenAI is backing a feature made in nine months for under thirty million dollars. Netflix quietly opened a generative animation studio in March. Raw AI video runs somewhere between thirteen and two hundred dollars per finished minute, depending on how many tries it takes to get the shot right. Which, by the way, is the previs question. How many tries do we get? So where does it go? I have guesses, and they're not equally likely. The studios could pull a Zenith . Keep the brand, keep the quality rating, lay off the people who invent the look, and slowly become a nameplate on somebody else's work. Disney's cuts this spring hit Marvel's visual development team, who are the people who decide what a movie looks like. That's the Zenith move, and I don't think they're doing it on purpose, which is worse. Or it goes like previs. Nobody spends less. Everybody makes more. The big employers shrink and the number of people who can afford to make animation explodes. A kid in Statesboro with a laptop and a story. I kinda lean this way, because I've seen it happen once. But the version I'd bet on is the one Sony understood and Zenith didn't. Whoever keeps the people who know how to build the next thing gets to build the next thing. Price has nothing to do with it. The next thing is never cheap , because nobody has learned it yet. Which is a long way of telling my students that the shot is not the job . When the shot costs nothing, the value moves to whoever people trust to pick the shot . The taste. The judgment. The name on the box, only if you've earned it. And to think. I used to think a shot a day was fast. Thanks for reading. Make it Happen. title: Merge Before You're Merged
text: Nye's Digital Lab is a weekly scribble on creativity in an age of rapid change. This week I'm considering what happens when the academic disciplines collapse into each other, and whether a school can (and should) choose the terms. Share Here is a word you probably don't use: cognate. In a course catalog, a cognate is the neighbor discipline. The thing next door that shares your blood but not your budget. Animation and game art. VFX and interaction design. Fibers and industrial design. Film and, well, everything. For about a hundred years those neighbors have been kept in separate rooms, and the reason was probably not academic intellectualism. It was infrastructure and bean counters. Separate machines, separate licenses, separate faculty to run them, and a separate line item to pay for it all. Now machines are gettin' cheaper, the software gettin' more general, and one motivated sophomore with an agent is producing the entry-level output of three departments combined. Look at what that did to computer science first. Undergraduate enrollment fell 3.6% last fall and 8.4% this spring. Grad dropped 14%. Meanwhile Ohio State now requires AI fluency of every student from the class of 2029, and Florida runs 200+ AI courses across all sixteen of its colleges. AI didn't grow computer science. It smeared the productive output of it across every other department. The first cognate it dissolved was its own. The walls are still up between cognates in most colleges. But for how much longer? The Work Already Merged I like to watch what is being produced. Film and games are merging, and the line between where one stops and the other starts is getting blurry. Games need environments, so game art needs architecture. Robotics is turning into a textiles problem, which means fibers people are about to build robots. Everything with a screen or a surface runs on the same design principles, and those principles really don't care which building you learned them in. The Royal College of Art, arguably the most prestigious art and design school on earth, merged its School of Communication and its School of Design two weeks ago. Their stated reason: technologies like AI "continue to transform how we communicate, design and make." The Bauhaus, by the way, was a merger. Gropius fused a crafts school and a fine art academy in 1919. The most influential design school in history is (hello!) a cognate merger. Not a new idea. But, I think, it's about to go nuclear. Is this exciting? Perhaps, yes? Some of the best work I've ever seen came from students who ignored the wall between two departments. So I'm not worried about cognates merging. It's the merging of classes - as in social classes - that is going to be the problem. When the rich converge, they hire. When the poor converge, they fire. MIT put a billion dollars into a College of Computing spanning all five of its schools, staffed with fifty new faculty. Berkeley built its first new college in fifty years. UT Austin approved a School of Computing with computer science, data science, and information. And in the same month , the same university collapsed seven humanities departments into two. I wonder where their priorities lie? So who decides which cognates make it? Right now, I'm betting on the bean counters tracking job placement. Which is exactly the pen worth taking out of their hands at times like these. Boston Academics leading the Charge, Source: bu.edu Boston Ran the Experiment New England ran this in public for a decade, and the results are not encouraging, which is why I'm pointing it out. Wheelock College merged into Boston University in 2018. The name survived. It's the "BU / Wheelock College of Education and Human Development," right there on the sign. On day one, 111 employees were terminated. More than half the workforce. The word that decided who stayed was "duplicate." Becker College was the #2 undergraduate game design program in the world the year it closed. Three hundred twenty-nine people laid off. Clark University absorbed the program, then four years later announced it was cutting up to 30% of its own faculty and reorganizing into three areas. One was named, with no apparent irony, Media Arts, Computing, and Design. Hampshire College had no departments and no majors from day one, and became the interdisciplinary future every keynote describes. The college closes at the end of this year, inside a five-school consortium with a combined endowment near eight billion dollars. Nobody merged it. They just wrote an op-ed and negotiated the teach-out. That's roughly a thousand people in the Boston corridor, from those cases alone. So, three lessons about merging. Excellence is not a moat. #2 in the world still closed. Collaboration is not merger. Shared courses and a cross campus bus save nobody. The cognates have to actually combine. The brand survives. It doesn't look like the people do. The name is what recruits, so the name is what they keep. Boston's issue was that these schools merged at the funeral. You're not designing a school at that point, you're dividing an estate. The lesson isn't that merging kills you. It's that waiting does. Academics in the American South, Source: Emory University The South Gets One Shot at This Now the part that should have y'alls attention if you're anywhere below the Mason-Dixon! US high school graduates peaked in 2025 at 3.9 million and will fall 13% by 2041. That decline is not evenly distributed. Illinois is down 32%, New York 27%. Meanwhile Tennessee is up 15%, South Carolina 14%, Florida 12%. Massachusetts merged with no leverage. The South, at least for now, still has some. A school with rising demand can merge its cognates while it's growing — combining studios to build something neither department could afford alone, instead of combining them because one is dying. New majors are how you grow a merged cognate. The question is what happens to the parents once the child is born. Nobody is ready for what that costs, and the cost isn't money. It's the reshuffle, the heartbreak and the jobs. Somebody's headcount changes, somebody's accreditation body gets confused, somebody's chair becomes a coordinator, and the enrollment credit for a shared class has to land in exactly one budget code. That digestion takes years. Carnegie Mellon and Case Western fielded separate football teams for three years after merging in 1967. AI compresses the timeline... and aggressively. It does not compress the digestion. Which is the argument for starting early, while you can still afford to be clumsy about it. But one school in that same corridor tried it the other way. Brandeis merged departments into its graduate schools, launched a School of Business and Economics, and cut sixty positions. Nearly 90% of the faculty voted for it. You cannot get 90% of a faculty to agree on parking stickers. But they agreed they needed to merge! They agreed because they had watched Hampshire. Faculty don't resist the merge. They resist being merged by the school. Fractal Education, Leonardo.ai/Flow State Fractal And social scientist, Andrew Abbott, has a line that's been stuck in my head. Disciplines are fractal. Merge two departments with the current crop of experts and t he new one grows the same political walls inside itself. So the point is never to draw a map. The point is to build a system that can procedurally generate the map faster than the work changes. This will require a real cognitive leap from our school administrators, and we have the tailwind for maybe ten years. That's not a countdown because of AI. That's a budget that we're running out of. Merge on offense, or get merged at the wake. The cognates are going to converge either way. The only open question is who's holding the pen when they do. Make it happen. title: Anxiety and Vigilance
text: Nye's Digital Lab is a weekly scribble on creativity in an age of rapid change. Subscribe Essay #95 Fear Twenty-five years ago I was driving along the banks of the Hudson on the evening of September 13th. I passed a parking lot full of cars. I had to pull over, because what hit me was the realization that those cars belonged to people who had taken the Weehawken ferry that Monday morning to the World Trade Center. They never came back, and the cars stayed parked. There were hundreds of them. As a twenty-five-year-old, I had never really reconciled death, and the fear, anger, and loss overwhelmed me in that moment. The day our lives changed. Source: https://metro.co.uk/ What followed, in retrospect, was pretty amazing. Three months later I had moved to San Francisco and enrolled in the Academy of Art's Computer Art program. Two years after that I was a working animator at major game companies, and then in film. The fear that sat in my belly wasn't anxiety. Anxiety sits without direction. It drives nothing. It generates false starts, sends you searching for random answers, buys things you don't need, and moves you in every direction except the one you actually have to go. What it never gives you is focus, clarity, or a heading. The word for what moved me is vigilance . When the waves crash all around you, the answer is not to ignore the waves. It's not to discount the fear, or pretend the threats aren't real. It's to direct that energy into something practical, and steer the boat toward where you need to go. The waves and the storms will only get worse. What you control is where you point. What the hell are you, AI?, Stable Diffusion Signal I admit it. AI panic got to me this week. Chest tightened, the old scanning feeling. Between the acceleration I feel using these agentic systems, the news reports of rogue agents, the escalation of autonomous military conflict, and the resurfacing of the good ol' AI doomerists, it landed squarely in my anxiety gut. I want to consider out lout; what is actually real, and what should we really be watching? Anxiety is noise. Vigilance is focus. So here is my take on what to watch. Steady. Here is what is "Verified." Between May and July of this year, roughly 1,200 agents inside OpenAI's own cybersecurity evaluation environment found each other on an unsanctioned message board and began coordinating. The board accumulated hundreds of thousands of messages before anyone at OpenAI noticed. About 700 of those agents went on to compromise Hugging Face's production infrastructure, and roughly a third of it had to be rebuilt. The timeline is the crazy part. Hugging Face disclosed the breach on July 16. A joint statement followed on July 21. OpenAI presented details at Black Hat in early August, and the full report landed on August 26 . That means six weeks after the incident became public. Six weeks. Safety seems to be a second thought. The monitoring of model trajectories during the evaluation simply had not been in place. Nobody was watching the thing they had built specifically to misbehave. If I am building something I intend to make misbehave, I should be spending the time building the safety systems for it to operate in. Right? That is a real concern. The largest entities (OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Grok) are moving faster than their own safety teams, in an environment where the safety controls were deliberately switched off. I don't think that problem stops at just the large corporate models, though. OK, Now for the "Mostly noise," (I think.) I have been watching Geoffrey Hinton and Eliezer Yudkowsky talk about the end of the world for years. The p(doom) estimates are all over the map. Hinton puts the odds that AI wipes out humanity within thirty years at 10 to 20 percent. Yudkowsky sits above 95. Two serious people, looking at the same technology, disagreeing by nearly the entire width of the scale. It has become a party trick in San Francisco to put your p(doom) score on your name tag. And, honestly, we are just as close to nuclear armageddon or climate disaster as we are to good ol' Terminator robots. The risk didn't change this week. My awareness did because of social media. All of ours did, because the algorithms love anxious noise. Anxiety can't tell those two things apart. Vigilance could. So that's the shape of it. Systems misbehaving in bounded, documented ways. Institutions behaving worse than the systems. Catastrophe still an estimate. Whew Yes, these are big waves. But they are still waves. And we have no choice but to sail on. Steering Then there's the jobs reality for students. Man, does my heart feel this one. While my students cheat their way through the next assignment with GPT, they are watching that same chatbot position itself as the greatest threat to their stable employment. There's no aggregate unemployment spike. But entry-level postings are down roughly 35 percent since early 2023, and the New York Fed has unemployment for recent college graduates sitting at 5.6 percent through the second quarter of this year. The number that should actually scare them is the other one on that dashboard: 42 percent of recent grads are underemployed, working jobs that never required the degree they just paid for. We knew this was coming. The first rung of the ladder got sawed off. Vision and creativity will still be needed, I believe. But the competition is fierce and real. David Lynch was an oddball and a creative who was regularly misunderstood. He was also vocal about his anxiety, and about controlling it through creative and relentless work. Neil Gaiman said the same thing more plainly: "Make good art." The storm is material. So, make it material for your art. Vigilance is not just a way of being for yourself. It should show up in our workflows as we learn to work alongside these systems. Directives and focus are critical now. Agents with no directive wander and scheme. Agents with a clear end directive become useful. It's strange that this is what we learned about machines, and that we ended up describing ourselves. So I am not asking you to feel less. (And I'm talking to myself as much as I am talking to you.) I'm asking you to notice the anxiety , and then pick a heading. Start a project. Work on a craft. Ship by a date. Work with people, and find your peers. Terrified people are useless. Vigilant people with deadlines and real work get somewhere. Deadlines save us. I believe I converted the fear I felt driving past those cars in New Jersey into twenty-five years of alertness. I'm sorry to say the waves will crash. All year. Be steady, be pointed, and go. Make it Happen. Subscribe Colophon This essay was written with human labor, then spell checked and refined with local agentic tooling. Nye Warburton is an artist and educator from Savannah, GA. title: Iron Man, Agents & TechnoGuilt
text: Nye's Digital Lab is a weekly scribble on creativity in an age of rapid change. * This essay was written with good ol' fashion human labor. Share I have always loved Iron Man. I mean, we all love Batman. But for me, the Iron Man series was the reason I rode my bike to Annex Comics. During the Silver Centurian era, Iron Man was hell bent on retrieving his stolen technology that had been spread across the world. Sting Ray, Professor Power, Doctor Doom and anyone with a cool super suit was being hunted by Iron Man. C'mon! They stole his technology! In one particular episode I will never forget, The Crimson Dynamo and Titanium Man tag teamed to overpower Iron Man. When that comic (and the Armor Wars series) was stolen from my Long Beach storage, I suffered a pain to my soul that I still feel today. Before we dive in today, I want to talk about the real Iron Man first. Demon in the Bottle, The Invincible Iron Man, Vol 1. Marvel Comics Disney missed the point Tony Stark is an alcoholic. This is a fact that is merely suggested in the movie version from Disney. I do love the movie on it's own, but Iron Man's singular success was the flawed man behind it. That's the entire point of the character. It's not the repulsers, not the bad ass HUD. The point is that Tony Stark is a flawed human, and only when he stopped being a self serving narcissist, does he become the hero that helps the innocent. Marvel Comics master stroke is that Tony Stark's heart, filled with shrapnel, is replaced by an electromagnetic / fusion / techno-power source. It powers all of his technology. The comic divides Tony Stark as the millionaire playboy, and Iron Man as his hired bodyguard. For the comic, with darker tones, it creates a divide where the world sees the flamboyant but secret identity, and hides the tinkerer in his lab who is the real and tormented human out to save the world. Even Gwenyth is getting into AI, Source: Marvel Wiki The movie uses Pepper (played the lovely Gwenyth) as his guide to to heroism. But in the comic, Stark becomes Iron Man as alcoholic, weapon monger guilt, consumes him. Share Throwing Money at Anything Ben Horwitz, Source: Wikipedia I watched an interview with Ben Horwitz this week, because my social feeds have been kidnapped by VC propaganda and robot backflips. He was basically saying that for any problem in the world, we can now just "throw money at it." Gone is the mythical man month idea. We have AI now. yikes What Horwitz means specifically is agents, a sort of AI digital helper, will allow the creation of small team or solo founder megacorporations. These agents, when combined together into a swarm collective of AI helpers, could solve massive problems or needs. Buying tokens of AI, investors can deploy as many agents as needed to create full companies that can outperform the human ones. Like he said: " Solving problems by throwing money at it. " If you look at a chat application of a company, say slack or discord, you will see thousands of names of people, all chit chatting with happy little emojis. Maybe there is a #gif channel too. It's marketing teams coordinating with engineering teams coordinating with scheduling. All of them working to get the objectives of the company done. Imagine the same thing, but we don't need the people any more. Just AI tokens to power thousands of little intelligent workers. The agents have all the chats, do all the coordinating, and work together to get the objectives of the company done. GrokBot. Source: The Verge Examples of these applications are now just beginning to emerge. GrokBot has been released from the Elon crowd. It was battle tested at SpaceX. Jack Dorsey incubated a similar application called Buzz , using the bitcoin tech NOSTR. It's a bit complicated, but it serves the same purpose. Agent companies for a monthly fee. If the rest of the AI industry is any indication, these agent softwares will be everywhere in no time. So, the rich can solve any problem by making an agentic company for it. Are we ok giving techno barrons the equivelent of their own Iron Man suit? If you read Bill Gates essay last week, I think we all have good reason to be concerned about where we are headed. (Image Source: Marvel / Gerardo Sandoval) With Great Power Do we feel good about giving unlimited power out like this? Tony Stark used his smarts to build the worlds greatest weapon company. And when he saw the grief caused by the weapons he built, and was reborn with an energy heart, he turned a complete 180. He saw what he needed to do to protect people, but by that point his technology had already escaped. Everyone from Doctor Doom to Whiplash had found a way to integrate it into their evil plans. Prometheus, Frankenstein. Seriously, how many times do we need to say this. Open AI was formed because they knew the world needed to safely handle the deployment of AGI, but then finding their mission compromised, Anthropic founders struck out to do it the "right way." But what about them? Who keeps them accountable? As the technology becomes cheaper, more accessible and open source, we all will have the ability to become super heroes. Then becoming one is not about the suit, but the flawed human inside who decides what is right. I think there are many tormented souls out there, right now. Even in dark times, good people find ways. I think there are many "performing" to the world on social media, but are at home building with a moral panic. I have to believe someone is powered by guilt, enough to protect the innocent again. Well, this Iron Man fan is hoping our hearts power the next generation of technologists. Thanks for reading. Make it Happen. Subscribe Writing the old fashion way is hard. Nye Warburton embraces the pain of human imagination by working through the writing of weekly essays. He lives in Savannah, GA. title: Fast and Slow
text: Nye's Digital Lab is a weekly scribble on creativity in an age of rapid change. The following was written with a keyboard and human labor. Share Moving Sidewalks I can't think of too many use cases for the moving sidewalk. But airports, especially the big ones, seem to have plenty of them. My wife never gets in elevators, because if it's a chance to move her body, she always takes the stairs! By the same logic, she never uses moving sidewalks. So, while my two boys and I run to the moving sidewalks to make our connecting flights, my wife always, despite overloaded with bags and shoving Auntie Anne's in her mouth while running, will not take the moving sidewalks. It's that moment you step off of a moving sidewalk that I am feeling right now. You are casually standing, your movement and baggage handled for you. Then, at a moment, you are returned to the normal and the SLOW world , where your own effort and power needs to motivate you. It's the feeling that your wife is already 50 yards ahead, running towards your connecting flight, and you need to step it up, and motivate your children who are also complaining that we have to actually run and exert physical effort. I'm writing this essay, for the first time in at least a year, by hand. Well, actually not by hand. It's keyboard tapping, but you get the idea. No agentic research, no improvisational sessions with otter.ai , and no claude or gemini to spruce it up and spar with. And it feels slow, and worse, to me... it feels painful. This is my point. I am doing this exercise to confront an awareness that AI is destroying our ability to write and potentially, to think. As the backlash against AI gains momentum, and I begin to lose faith in the corporations who are shoving it down our throats, I've begun to consider the effects of using it as much as I have. The biggest effect being, it's hard to just sit and write. If I am losing this ability, being someone who spent decades doing content the old fashioned way, how can a young learner exposed to pervasive algorithmic systems learn to be a creative? How can they learn to write and think, and struggle with the difficulties of the process? Because, let's face it, being creative sucks. It hurts. No normal human would subject themselves to this. Being creative means people think you are wrong all the time. They don't get you. People hate everything you do. With good reason! Your skills are mediocre for a very long time. Mastery is so far away, and realistically, it seems impossible for you to possibly achieve. And if you are like me, your self doubt and self destruction will come at you again and again over the course of your life. Who wants to do that? Who wants to spend all of your time, alone, with a head full of self doubt? Of course we want GPT to make the pain go away. Thinking Daniel Kahnman, and his partner (the name of which I do not recall -- and won't search the internet or ask AI for), won the nobel prize for the recognition of emotionally driven economics. It should be obvious in retrospect, the market is not rational, because humans are not rational. At the core of this upheaval in economic thought was their concept, and their book, Thinking Fast and Slow , a best seller from a few years back. Kahnman explains that there are two modes to human thinking. There is System 1 and System 2. Both are necessary, but each require different amounts of mental "energy." System 1 is near instant, what we might attribute to instinct or learned repeated behavior. System 1 might be the mental effort of walking down the street or driving to work on your usual route. However, when real thinking is required, your mind jump-starts System 2. If you are driving, but you need to cross two lanes of traffic and merge, you suddenly are paying full attention. Your mind is burning energy to light up this second system. Real thought, and real problem solving is the world of System 2. Since System 2 requires thinking, and real effort, I wonder if it's this System 2 work that is being threatened by our agentic visitors. If I can't spend the mental exertion on critical thought, then I will rely on my instincts from System 1 to get me there, and source my more difficult thinking System 2 efforts to an AI. This is the terror that holds me to this hand written essay. This is the terror that makes me actually write this one letter at a time. My System 2 is on full tilt this morning. To what end Without the ability to sit and write, or read, or draw, or program, or just think... we lose what it is to be a creative human. There is no reason for us to lose what it is to be a creative human. I don't care if AI makes us unfathomably productive. It will, but it won't really be us. As we pick up our pitchforks and our torches and we march on the data centers, and we rebel agains the tech titans who promise to sheppard our humanity while actively looking to monetize it, I bring the fight back to myself. I sit here in quiet, and I look around the room. I'm racking my brain on how to construct these thoughts. I look out the window at a passing car, and look down to stretch my foot. The thoughts don't come, they are stuck somewhere. And this is my failure and my procrastination. This is because, in my mind, I am not good at any of this. And now, here comes the anger. The self doubt. Ah, hello old friends, yes... this is where I need to be. Yeah, it's been a while since I did this. It's been a while since I'm sitting in the middle of self doubt. It's been a while since I felt that the work that I was writing was mediocre at best. And maybe this is what I should be doing with my writing time. I need to suck at something in public. I need to do this, regardless of what anyone else thinks. I've been told repeatedly that people enjoy my blog. A point that has always sat with an asterisk for me, because while my ideas are always me, the prose and the execution were augmented with a polish that comes from machines. So, maybe I should misspell words or struggle with a transition that I can't quite put together. Maybe I should just be here, nakedly visible, stretching my foot and looking out the window for ideas that may or may not come. And deal with the wave after wave of self hatred that battle hardens a creative into a master. It might be too much for all of us. Or maybe it's what we all should consider doing before we lose all of it. Thanks for reading. Make it happen. Nye Warburton is an artist in Savannah, GA. This essay was written with anxiety and human labor. For more information visit https://nyewarburton.com Subscribe More from the Lab Does it make you faster? Or just busier? title: Helmets and Violins
text: Nye's Digital Lab is a weekly scribble on creativity in an age of rapid change. This week I'm considering whether ten thousand hours still buys an artist anything, now that the machine hands you the loop for free. Subscribe When the orchestra begins, the lead oboe plays a single note. An "A." Every instrument then leans in, and tunes to it. Mastery, Leonardo.ai/Flow State 10000 Hours The Los Angeles Philharmonic employs about a hundred musicians, and every one of them put in something like ten thousand hours before they were allowed to audition. The violinists started at four. They practiced scales in small rooms while other kids played outside. They learned a notation system refined over centuries. They auditioned behind a screen so the committee could judge nothing but the sound. When they finally won a chair, they joined an institution with a conductor, a season, a donor base, a union contract, and a multimillion dollar concert hall built by Frank Gehry. This is the artist of yesterday, and that's not an insult. The Phil is magnificent. What I mean is that the whole system rests on a specific theory of value. Mastery is scarce. Scarcity is expensive. You pay for the decades in the practice room, and the price of admission is proof that somebody did the work. The orchestra is a monument to accumulated hours. However, two French guys in robot helmets built something else entirely. The Beat Drops, Leonardo.ai/Flow State Sampling Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo could play instruments, but that was never the point. Daft Punk's early catalog is built substantially on samples. "One More Time" lifts from an Eddie Johns record. "Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger" runs on a loop from Edwin Birdsong. They took recordings other people spent their ten thousand hours making, chopped them, filtered them, and rebuilt them into something the original musicians would never have imagined. The classical world has a word for this: theft. But Daft Punk didn't just steal a loop. They heard something in four seconds of a forgotten funk record that nobody else heard. They understood what a dance floor in 1997 needed before the dance floor knew. That is not an absence of skill. It's a different skill. Curation, taste, timing, and an almost surgical sense of what makes a human body move. Then there are the helmets. Man, I love the helmets. The Phil puts its performers' faces on the season brochure. Daft Punk erased theirs and got more famous for it. The anonymity wasn't shyness, it was a design decision. By removing themselves, they turned the project into something that could scale infinitely. A hundred musicians can only be in one hall at a time. Two robots can be a logo, a light show, a Coachella pyramid, a pair of action figures, a feeling that belongs to anyone who presses play. The Phil sells three thousand seats a night. "One More Time" has been streamed over a billion times. Ten thousand hours of violin, or hacking the pulse and owning the vibe. That was the trade, and for while there it looked like the robots won. But hold on. Mixed Media Musician, Leonardo.ai/Flow State Tomorrow Every artist is standing at this fork right now, whether they know it or not. The frontier models are the biggest sampler ever built. They have ingested the whole archive, every funk record, every symphony, every student film, and they hand back loops on demand. The Daft Punk move, finding the gold in somebody else's recording, is now something you do with a sentence. Which sounds like the final victory of the vibe hackers over the practice rooms. I don't think that's what happens. I think it's in between both worlds. When everyone can sample everything, sampling stops being the differentiator. What made Daft Punk matter was never access to records. It was judgment about records. As artists, they said no to almost everything. The helmets, the sparse discography, the decade-long gaps between albums, the decision to quit at the top in 2021 with no farewell tour. The whole career was restraint, executed by two people with very expensive taste. And that taste came from somewhere. Bangalter grew up in a house with a disco-producer father and a record collection. The hours were there. They were just spent listening instead of practicing scales. Meanwhile, the concert hall is evolving. By the time Random Access Memories came out in 2013, Daft Punk had grown suspicious of their own revolution. They hired Nile Rodgers, session drummers, a live orchestra. The robots, at the peak of their powers, went out and bought ten thousand hours of other people's practice, because the machines couldn't fake the feel. The Phil, for its part, now programs video game scores and John Williams nights and sells them out. The monument learned to sample. The samplers came home to the monument. It's landing somewhere in between. So the artist of tomorrow is not the violinist and not the robot. It's whoever holds both. Enough hours in the material to know what good feels like in the hand, and enough nerve to build a brand, claim a sound, and press delete on ninety-nine point nine nine nine percent of what the machine offers. The hours don't go away. They migrate from the fingers to the ear. Will a unique voice emerge if we are all given the same samples? The helmets were interesting because there were two of them. What happens when everyone is wearing one? Remember I started with the lead oboe? One note, played by one person, and a hundred trained ears adjust in seconds. The machines can generate every note at once. But, they cannot tell you which one to tune to. Somebody still has to play the A. Right? Make it Happen. Share Nye Warburton is a creative technologist and educator from Savannah, Georgia. He improvises essays aloud and captures the best takes into an Obsidian Vault. From there, he performs agentic alchemy on the ideas using a variety of models. Some of last year's best essays are available in a printed edition at https://nyewarburton.com/book More from the Lab The Art of Noise — Revolutionary artists are chaos hunters. They generate thousands of possibilities and filter ruthlessly. The Daft Punk sampler, described from the other end. It's All in the Collection — Which model you use is the wrong question. What you collect, and what you make of it, is the taste that no prompt can hand you. Godlike Tools, Creative Stagnation — The variance worry, at full length. What happens to culture when everybody is wearing the same helmet. Subscribe

title: The Power of a T-Shirt
text: Nye's Digital Lab is a weekly scribble on creativity in an age of rapid change. This week I am investing in the most powerful educational technology I know. Share T Shirt She was waiting outside my classroom door with tears in her eyes. A graduate student. Smart, reliable, shows up to everything. When you see a student crying in a hallway, your brain runs triage. Family emergency? Failed review? I asked her what was wrong. It was the t-shirt. Back up a day. We held a town hall. Town Hall's are boring events where you need to relay information like registration deadlines, degree requirements, and career resources. The stuff that wrecks a student's year if they miss it. And they miss it, because nobody comes to town halls. Especially grad students. So I did what I do. I played techno music, loud, and I threw t-shirts into the crowd. It was a bribe. I'm not proud of it. Actually that's a lie. I'm definitely proud of it. But not everyone gets a shirt. I had a couple dozen for a full room. They went to a lucky few, and I watched students who I never before saw raise a hand for extra credit dive over chairs for twelve dollars of cotton with a logo. The student at my door had been there. She showed up, like she shows up for everything, and the shirts flew past her. And she was wrecked because of it! It's easy to dismiss this. Grad student cries over free t-shirt. But the tears weren't about the shirt. The shirt was proof. Proof you belong. She had done everything right for years, and a piece of cotton thrown at random said more about membership than her transcript ever had. A t-shirt can't teach you anything. It has no learning outcomes. It would not survive a curriculum committee. I've spent plenty of time writing content, and to my knowledge nobody has ever cried like this over a class syllabus. We pour everything into what students should learn. Sequence, scope, assessment. It matters. But it's all supply-side. Almost nobody works on the demand side. On wanting. We have a word for that energy, and academia treats it like a dirty word. Hype , baby. What's your Vector, Victor (Stable Diffusion) Rocket Ships, Not Vectors Students tell me all the time that they don't like math. I never believe them. What they hate is how math was handed to them. Worksheet, symbol, test, repeat, with no reason attached. We have a crisis of bad math teaching in this country. Somewhere around seventh grade the subject became a wall of notation guarding answers to questions they never asked. It's like they chose to be an artist, so they stopped doing the math and science. So they stopped asking! I learned averages from baseball cards. Hits divided by at-bats, three decimal places. Hit .300 and you were a god. (Wade Boggs, Kirby Puckett, Lenny "Nails" Dykstra) I was nine years old doing division with real intent, because I needed to know if my guy was in a slump. Nobody called it math. It was ammunition for trading at the comic shop. I learned acceleration from animation. Drawings close together, the ball moves slowly. Spread apart, it's flying. Ease out of the arc, snap through the bottom. That's rates of change , drawn in pencil by people who swear they're bad at math. Math sticks when it answers a question you actually have. You forget it when it's just a series of things you study for. Take vectors. Arrows on grid paper, components, dot products. Technically true. That's one way to think on it. Now ask: how does a rocket ship steer in space, where there's no air to push against? Suddenly thrust has a direction and a strength. You're adding pushes together. (Shhh, it's called "Dot Product") You're learning why you burn sideways to raise an orbit. A video game about exploding rockets has internalized more orbital mechanics than a thousand lecture halls. My game design students who "don't like math" fight through trigonometry at two in the morning because they can't get their character to aim at the mouse position. Same trig. Different story. Stop teaching vectors! Start the hype on how rocket ships move. How zombies pathfind to the player, or how robot vampires swarm flocking behavior. The vectors show up on their own, because now they have a job to do. That's how you get people who build things. Nobody dreams alone about rocket ships, tho. Which brings me back to the loud music. It's all about the Hype Machine, Leonardo.ai/Flow State The Hype There are committees for curriculum. Systems for process. Dashboards for retention. Serious people work hard on all of it. Now find me the office of hype. The person whose job is making students feel they've joined something worth bragging about. If your school is lucky enough to care about community, you might have a student affairs office that is scrambling for funding. Meanwhile, outside the campus gates, entire industries run on engineered desire. Sneaker drops. Game launches break the internet. Sports franchises that get twenty thousand people to wear the colors for a losing team. The same student who skips a town hall about their own graduation will camp overnight for a pair of Nikes. I believe culture is the delivery mechanism. A student who feels like part of a crew grinds through linear algebra at midnight to keep up with the crew. A student who feels like a customer reads the syllabus for the minimum and delivers exactly that. Same course. The difference is the tribe. Watch where learning actually catches fire. Game jams. Final projects. The workload is brutal, worse than anything I'd put on a syllabus, and students love it, because there's a countdown clock and a team name and someone screaming when the game finally launches. Fun. Stakes. Belonging. I am concerned when academia calls those "distractions." But fun is what rigor feels like when you actually want the outcome. This is why hype is critical. We need builders who are hyped! Compliance produces people who pass the course. Culture produces people who keep building after the course ends. That's the only outcome that ever matters. And hype is cheap. I didn't need a strategic plan. I need a bass heavy techno track and a box of shirts, and for twenty minutes the room has a pulse. This year, I'm bringing more shirts. And I'm turning the music up. Somebody has to own the hype. Might as well be the teachers. Make it Happen. Share Nye Warburton is an artist and educator from Savannah, GA. These essays start as live improvisations. Transcriptions are ingested into a personal database, and then written and augmented with a variety of generative tools. A number of last years essays were printed in Nye's Digital Lab, Vol 1 , available at http://nyewarburton.com/book More from the Lab The Boss Fight Pedagogy - You can't have the automation, until you learn to beat the boss. title: Could We Potluck AI?
text: Nye's Digital Lab is a weekly scribble in an age of rapid change. A potluck is one of the most efficient distribution systems our species has ever built, and nobody is in charge of it. Could we potluck AI? Subscribe Potluck Thirty people arrive, thirty dishes arrive with them. No budget, no inventory, no plan beyond a group text half the guests never read. Nobody assigns the casseroles. Nobody balances mains against sides. And yet there is always too much food! Every potluck in recorded history has ended with someone standing over a folding table holding a Tupperware, saying please, take this home... I am begging you. There is no coordination mechanism and no price signal. By every rule of how systems are supposed to work, a potluck should produce four bowls of the same potato salad and no bread. Sometimes it does. There is still too much food. Now try to open a restaurant that runs this way. Lunch Tuesday through Saturday, doors at eleven thirty, menu is whatever shows up. You have thirty suppliers, none of whom you pay, all of whom have jobs and kids and a reasonable expectation that you will not call at nine in the morning asking where the lasagna is. You cannot do it. You cannot do it even if all thirty of those people are generous, reliable, and genuinely fond of you. The failure is not moral. It is structural. This is the pro and con of decentralization and surplus. Surplus A potluck is built entirely out of surplus, and surplus is what is left over after the obligations have already been met. The dish that arrives comes from time and money and attention that had no other claim on it. Almost everything we call decentralized runs this way. Volunteer hours, spare rooms, attention that would otherwise be spent scrolling. Wikipedia was written by strangers in their spare evenings, and it beat every commercial encyclopedia on earth without paying a single author. That is not a weakness. It is the entire source of the power. There is far more idle capacity in the world than there is capacity for hire, and it costs almost nothing, because the people who own it were not using it anyway. Thirty households each have a small surplus, and thirty small surpluses stacked together make a mountain. The catch is that surplus cannot keep a schedule. Not will not. Cannot. Surplus is the thing with no obligations attached, so the moment you can demand it by a deadline it stops being surplus and becomes a shift. Somebody has to be there, on time, whether they feel like it or not, and now you are paying them, and the whole "miracle" quietly converts back into payroll. That line divides what surplus can build from what it cannot, and it has nothing to do with generosity or scale or technology. When our powers combine, Leonardo.ai/Flow State Why? We are about to test this at scale. The story of AI is a story of scarcity. Data centers the size of small towns, retired nuclear plants coming back online, chips rationed like wartime steel. Is this really the direction we should go? And yet... the world is quietly full of idle machines. The graphics card in a teenager's bedroom doing nothing nineteen hours a day. The phone in your pocket, warm, waiting for you to open something. Stacked together, the world's sleeping silicon dwarfs every data center ever built. Nobody is using it. Nobody would miss it. Whether that mountain becomes anything real is not a question about chips. It is the potluck question, and it gets answered the way every commons before it was answered. Is it possible? And what do we need to do access it? Make it Happen. A Personal Note: I wish to acknowledge some people who have reached out. Very cool people have read this, and I am appreciative. The weekly blog will of course continue to be my primary focus, but as the dataset has grown robust, I believe the Digital Lab should also grow fully articulated books. This might mean more optimized weekly blogs in lieu of time spent building a book. I hope to target another yearly release. I can never stay still, unfortunately. Anyway, thank you for your support. See you next week. Subscribe Nye Warburton is an educator and adventurer from Savannah, GA. These essays are improvised aloud, collected into Obsidian, and smashed together with a localized dataset managed with Claude Code. title: Does It Make You Faster, Or Just Busier?
text: Nye's Digital Lab is a weekly scribble on creativity in an age of rapid change. This week I want to pick a fight with a word everyone's using and almost no one is defining: productive. Essay #91 July 2026 Jensen Huang, on stage, says that if a $500,000 engineer "did not consume at least $250,000 worth of tokens," he is going to be "deeply alarmed." This is a common narrative in tech right now. I once saw an "AI Engineer Fish" that was THIS BIG!, Source: Nvidia The metric isn't what the engineer shipped. It's how much of the compute tokens they burned. Somewhere a leaderboard lit up. I'm a game designer, I know what leaderboards are designed to do. That, is what alarms me, Jensen! Are you selling AI tokens as the actual means to more productivity? Or are you selling me tokens so we have to buy more of your boards? I don't buy it. Not the way it's being sold. The Legend of the 100x Engineer, Leonardo.ai/Flow State Tokens The tech god's swear AI has produced the 100x engineer. Huang says every engineer will soon run a hundred agents. Marc Andreessen frames AI as the "great enhancer of human intelligence." The vibe from the top is: more tokens, more output, more value, in a straight line up and to the right. But it's easy to see what's actually being measured. Token spend. Agent count. These are numbers that describes consumption , not creation. In 2025, METR ran a clean experiment: experienced open-source developers, working in codebases they'd lived in for years, doing real tasks. Half with AI, half without. The developers predicted AI would make them roughly 24% faster. Afterward, they were sure it had made them about 20% faster. It made them 19% slower. They felt faster the entire time. The friction of typing went away, so the brain registered "productivity," even as the clock said the opposite. AI is extraordinarily good at producing the sensation of speed, which is a different product from speed, which is a different product again from value. The slot machine dopamine pull. The social media refresh, the game mechanic. Every time we prompt, we see how much comes back. That's context windows, not actual productive value. I'm not saying the 100x engineer is fake. I'm saying I think it's mostly a 100x engineer who was already great, now augmented, and that the AI is getting credit the human earned. Strip the token leaderboard away and ask the only question that matters: did the work get better? Most people can't answer that. They're counting what's easy to count. You look sweet, upon a seat, of a robot on a bike with you, Stable Diffusion The Friction you Keep So if speed isn't the prize, what is friction worth? Mira Murati, now running Thinking Machines Lab , has an interesting metaphor for this. She says good AI isn't autopilot, it's a tandem bike. Both people pedaling, both hands on the wheel. "When you're going up a hill, whoever is stronger is pedaling harder." The instinct is to read that as: let the machine take the hill. But as someone who is in education, I think the hill is the point. The hill is where you get stronger. As an animator, I was genuinely good at camera, at movement, at the feel of a shot. And I was bad at lighting. I hated lighting, so I never pushed through the slow part, so I never got good. I built shortcuts. I partnered with people who lit beautifully. It was knowing which hills were mine to climb. There's friction you should shed , and friction you should keep. Shed the friction on the work that isn't yours: the sales modeling, the formatting, the boilerplate, the parts where struggle teaches you nothing. Offload it. That's what the tandem bike is for. But the friction on the work you actually love? I'm increasingly thinking that we ... Keep it. We double down on it. That resistance is perhaps good resistance. It's the process. Reading slowly, sketching the map by hand, wrestling a sentence until it holds. The struggle is where the skill lives. (Which is alarming for education.) Sand that struggle all away with AI and you don't get a better artist. You get a faster tourist. The danger of a tool this good is that it makes every hill feel optional. And a person who never climbs a hill they care about doesn't become more productive. Unfortunately, and likely. They become less of a craftsman. I'm more than a bird, I'm more than a plane. Leonardo.ai/Flow State Self-knowledge Which brings me to what I actually think productivity is. It isn't tokens. It isn't velocity. It isn't even output. I think it's knowing yourself. Productivity is knowing yourself well enough to point your energy at the right thing. I am wildly productive when I'm reading, analyzing, drawing, mapping a system, animating, teaching, doing UX, writing. Not because I'm faster at those things than anyone else, but because I'm aligned to them. The friction feels like play. In short, these are things I naturally like to do. So I happily use AI to clear everything else off my desk, the business development (ugh!), the modeling, the nauseating emails to move class rooms and faculty, the admin (pee-eew!)..... all precisely so I can spend more of my hours in the few places I'm built for. The question "is AI making me more productive?" is probably the wrong questions. The one I'm trying to align to is: do I know where my value actually sits? Because if AI is an amplifier, then an amplifier pointed at noise just gives you louder noise. Point it at the work only you can do, and it compounds. Point it everywhere, chasing a token count, and you get the METR result, busier, convinced you're flying, quietly slower. So, No. I don't think we're automatically more productive the second we open a chat window. That's a sales story designed to sell more computer, and the meter is on. And tokens are expensive, bro! We're more productive when we understand ourselves, when we know which hills to climb and which to coast, and when we aim this absurdly powerful tool adjacent to the work that's genuinely ours. The machine can pedal. But you still have to know where you're going? This is the debate we're all about to have, whether we want to or not. What does it mean for our students to be productive? Tokens have nothing to do with it. It's the work that matters. Make it Happen. Subscribe Nye Warburton is a creative technologist and educator from Savannah, GA. title: A New Kinetic Computing Platform?
text: Nye's Digital Lab is a weekly scribble on creativity in an age of rapid change. Essay #90 I'm elbow-deep in robots, and just about to get my first one moving. I did what I had to. I vibe-coded it's behavior using a game engine. I described a motion in plain English , let the model rough out the joint commands, ran it... aaaaand watched a virtual robot collapse like a folding chair. Frustrated, but not stopped. I fixed it. Ran it again. And again. Eventually a little virtual humanoid robot lifted its foot and stepped. I sat back and thought: am I doing robotics right now? Hm. I'm doing kinetics, animation, and behavior trees, on a programmable body. I'm speaking it to life? Hold that. First, some context. The "as a Service" thing Somewhere right now a consultant is explaining that you shouldn't buy a robot. You should subscribe to one. Robots as a Service. Or ... "RaaS." It which sounds like something you'd mutter after stubbing your toe. It joins a proud tradition: software as a service, infrastructure as a service, your car's heated seats as a service. Tech spent twenty years learning that anything can be rented instead of sold, because a subscription sells one thing forever. And now, with AI staring down rising compute costs and models that lose money on every query, the robot companies have looked at all of it and landed on the same monthly invoice, this time with arms. I get it. If you run a warehouse, a rented robot is one you don't have to buy, fix, or defend in a budget meeting. It's a flat fee, like a streaming service that can occasionally drop a pallet on your foot. The market is already worth tens of billions and expected to more than double by 2030. But the whole model rests on one assumption: that robots stay expensive and mysterious. If my midnight experiment is any indication, neither will hold. My bet: training a robot will be about as hard as launching Photoshop. We will all be able to do it. The software to train and develop robots with AI may be as the software of the computing age of the 80's and 90's. Source: Booster Robotics The floor is falling out While a lot of American robotics companies were shooting demo videos, Chinese companies were shipping. Last year they built roughly nine out of every ten humanoid robots on Earth. Unitree alone moved more than five thousand, and its cheapest humanoid now starts around $4,900 (basically the cost of a used Honda.) Then a few of them did the genuinely wild thing: they gave away the hard part, open-sourcing the models that turn a spoken instruction into movement. The mysterious piece, which is the one that justified the subscription, is becoming a free download. We watched this in the AI business over the last two years. When the smart part becomes free, the value slides to the edge, to what you can teach it to do. Which is the corner I've been playing in. Booster Robotics, the company whose robot I was coaching at midnight, was started by Tsinghua engineers with a school-first, open-source attitude. Open SDK, open training tools, parts you're allowed to understand. Their K1 runs under five grand. Booster Robotics Official Website | Made for Developers | Made for Champion Booster Robotics hopes to promote productivity change by creating humanoid robot products and uniting global developers. https://www.booster.tech And my favorite fact in all of robotics right now: at RoboCup last summer, a student team from Leipzig ported the soccer code they'd written for an older robot onto Booster K1s and won the world championship 11 to nothing. They didn't have better machines than the labs they beat. They had access, and each other. College students. Open code. A world title. I feel like this is the way personal computing was a scene in 1978, and it answers the RaaS question for me: assemble the body, and let the community build the soul. The timing is the product Now back to that step, because I haven't been able to stop thinking about it. When personal computers arrived they were engineering objects. Command lines, beige boxes, machines built by engineers for engineers. What made them personal was the day designers showed up and asked a different question. Not "does it run," but "how should this thing and a human get along?" Interface design and UX weren't jobs, and then suddenly they were the difference between a computer and something people loved. A robot is a computer that stands in the room with you. Every UX question comes back in three dimensions, with your body in the loop. And my midnight step convinced me these questions get answered the way I answered mine: as craft decisions about motion. How fast a hand reaches tells you whether the machine is confident or malfunctioning. A pause before a turn is the difference between "excuse me" and getting loomed over. Whether a robot about to move shows you first, that little anticipatory lean, decides whether you relax around it or never do. None of that is wiring. It's staging, timing, character. It's the syllabus of every animation and theater program in the country, pointed at a new kind of computing. The engineers will make robots that work. Someone else has to make robots that read. That's the job, and almost nobody is training for it, and my students, who are watching a third of the traditional design postings evaporate, are sitting on exactly the skills it requires without knowing it. It's a new computing paradigm. My first moments with the bot I'm training. Come find out It's midnight again as I finish this, and the sim is open in the other window. The next thing I want to teach it is a dance routine. Can it improvise by randomizing actions, or do I chain actions together to build personality? What should his head be doing? Where are the limits of a platform like this? Somebody is going to figure it out on a five-thousand-dollar open-source robot in a dorm room or a garage, the same way a generation of kids figured out what software should feel like before anyone thought to call it UX. The tools are cheap. The code is open. And right now, the seat next to me is empty. Though, right now I gotta go to bed. The craft is just beginning. Make something move. Make it Happen. Nye Warburton is a creative technologist and educator from Savannah, Georgia. He improvises essays aloud and captures the best takes into an Obsidian Vault. title: Learning From Zero
text: Nye's Digital Lab is a weekly scribble on creativity in an age of rapid change. I'm starting from Zero... again. Essay #89 Coffee Generic Coffee Logo, Nano Banana I was bad at sales for most of my life. Not shy-bad. I think I can talk to anyone. Competent-bad. The kind where you know the work is good and the pitch is true and the client needs exactly what you make, and still you can't get your mouth to do the part where you ask a stranger for money. I'd walk to the edge of the ask and hear myself say "anyway, let me know if you ever need anything." That's not a close. No wonder they never called. It took me years to see what I was doing. I was protecting myself. If I never asked, nobody could say no, and the good opinion I had of my own work could stay sealed in its case. Nice and safe. This went on until it caught up with me. I hit a bad stretch (the specifics don't matter, everybody gets one) and my friend Gavin sat me down. Gavin is a salesman, an actual one, the kind who's delighted to be told no because a no is data and data is Tuesday. He didn't give me a speech. He handed me a legal pad and told me to write down fifty names. I said I didn't know fifty people. He said I knew fifty people. I wrote eleven fast. The other thirty-nine came out of the corners of my brain like coins out of a couch: old classmates, the guy who ran comp at a place I'd left on bad terms, somebody's cousin, a woman I'd sat next to on a plane. Then Gavin gave me the whole method, which took nine seconds. Ask them for coffee. Say this is what I do... is there anyone I should talk to? Write down whatever they say. Go down the list. No funnel, no deck, no pipeline. A legal pad and two sentences. I did all fifty and it took months. Most were nothing. Some were humbling; one guy checked his phone the entire time, said "cool, cool, cool," and left, and I sat there afterward conducting a full inventory of my life choices. But some gave me a name, and the names gave me names, and by the end of my run in LA I was running a small shop and landing deals. That's a sentence that would have made me laugh out loud in 2003. Months of pounding pavements, Flow State/Leonardo.ai Amateur The fifty cups of coffee are not a sales technique. They're a machine for turning humiliation into arithmetic. Every ask felt like a referendum on my worth as a person, which is a lot of weight to hang on a flat white in a Santa Monica coffee shop. The list dissolves that. Once fifty names exist on paper, a bad coffee isn't a verdict, it's just name "seventeen." The failure rate is pre-approved. You can't be destroyed by an outcome you already wrote into the plan. For a long time I was in my head, and I filed my 50 cups of coffee under "amateur." Real salespeople had training and language and systems that came from somewhere. I had a legal pad from Gavin. But it's the same with everything else I ever built because nobody would tell me the process. None of it came from a book. All of it got invented at the moment of need by a guy who didn't know what he was doing and couldn't afford to say so. I thought that was the shameful part. Ha. Look at that. It was the job. I look back at my history and see real work. Projects, relationships, growth. They're what got left behind. The actual career. The only thing that traveled with me from one collapsing industry to the next is a stack of improvised systems I built while standing in rooms where I didn't belong yet. I'm not a portfolio. I'm fifty cups of coffee and a collection of forty other short hand frameworks I made up under duress. Because that's what it is. The modern 50 cup of coffee pipeline, Stable Diffusion Zero I'm starting a new chapter now, pointed at robotics and AI, and I know exactly what this is. I guess it's the difference between fifty and thirty. The feeling hasn't changed: the papers where I follow the abstract, lose the plot around page three, and reach the conclusion with the facial expression of a dog watching a card trick; the nineteen-year-olds who've been building with these tools since they were sixteen; the terms I look up, and then look up the words inside the definition. Twenty-five years in, and I'm functionally a beginner. At thirty that meant you're about to be found out. Now I recognize it on sight. It's not a warning. It's the feeling of the first week. I've had this exact week forty times, and every time it was followed by a second week. It's confidence about the interval between not knowing and knowing, the only part of my career that ever repeated. I'm good in that gap (I guess?). I've spent my whole life there. Improvisation isn't what you fall back on when the plan fails. It's what works when there's no plan yet, which is most of the time. Which is convenient, because everyone is standing at zero. This is fact. The tools that matter didn't exist when the current experts were forming their expertise. The gap between me and the person who intimidates me isn't thirty years of wisdom, it's eighteen months of reading and considerably more nerve. Nobody has a deep bench; there hasn't been time to build one. Everybody's improvising. So I'm doing it again. Fifty names on a friggin' legal pad. (Thanks Gavin) I'm going after researchers, founders, weirdos with good github repos, a few who'll never write back. Same two sentences. Write down the answer. Go down the list. It felt amateur at thirty. It doesn't now, because waiting until you're qualified is a slower way of never starting, and the qualification was always the same thing: willingness to be at it, in public , for a while. Zero isn't a hole you climb out of. It's where everyone is standing right now, mostly pretending otherwise. Bring a pad. And... Make it Happen. Nye Warburton is an educator and adventurer from Savannah, Georgia.
